ote.title: Events in an open format (OTE)
ote.description: Open Tech Events (OTE) is an initiative driven by Community Builders to publish each community's events in a shared, open format. It exists so event data is not locked inside closed platforms: with a single file, any directory, website or bot can read your agenda. If your community publishes one, this directory will show your upcoming events automatically.
ote.waysTitle: How to generate your OTE file
ote.way0: Register the community and its events on eventos.wiki: the easiest route, it generates the OTE file for you.
ote.way1: Use the ote-tools agent skills so an agent writes the spec for you.
ote.way2: Create the events by hand with the OTE web editor.
ote.way3: Start from ote-template, a repo with several tools already wired up.

web.title: Website URL
web.description: Add the community's main website or most stable landing page.
web.bullet0: Examples: own website, official page or persistent microsite.
web.bullet1: If you've already used it as the main URL, there's no need to repeat it here.

eventsUrl.title: Events URL
eventsUrl.description: Link to the platform where they post events or tickets.
eventsUrl.bullet0: Examples: Meetup, Eventbrite, Luma, saraos.tech, Google Calendar or own agenda.
eventsUrl.bullet1: Use it when activity mainly lives on that calendar or platform.

linkAggregator.title: Link aggregator
linkAggregator.description: Link to a page that brings together several profiles or resources of the community.
linkAggregator.bullet0: Examples: Linktree, Beacons, Bento or similar page.
linkAggregator.bullet1: Useful when the community centralizes its presence in a single aggregator.

mailingList.title: Mailing list
mailingList.description: Link to subscribe or view the community's mailing list.
mailingList.bullet0: Examples: Google Groups, Buttondown, Substack or Mailchimp.
mailingList.bullet1: Add it if email is a relevant channel for following activity or interacting with other members.

eventosWiki.description: The community's page on eventos.wiki, the open directory of tech events in Spain.

ote.description: URL of the events file in Open Tech Events format. This is what lets the directory show your upcoming events.

blog.title: Blog
blog.description: The community's blog or articles section, if separate from the main site.
blog.bullet0: If the blog is the website itself, just fill in the Web field.

rss.title: RSS feed
rss.description: RSS or Atom feed to follow the community's posts.

forum.title: Forum
forum.description: Discussion forum or wiki the community keeps open, if any.

status.title: How to choose the status
status.description: Use the status based on the community's recent activity.
status.bullet0: Active: there are people running the community and it has had recent activity.
status.bullet1: Inactive: for meetups, usually applies if there has been no activity for more than a year; for conferences, if it has exceeded its usual cadence.
status.bullet2: Unknown: use it if it's unclear.

communityType.title: How to choose the type
communityType.description: Choose the main type that best describes how the community operates.
communityType.techMeetup: Periodic meetups, usually in talk format and contained size.
communityType.conference: Typically annual event, larger and with several talks or tracks.
communityType.umbrellaOrg: Groups local communities under a common brand or structure.
communityType.hacklab: Maker community with physical space and shared resources.
communityType.collaborativeGroup: People who collaborate on projects, events, content or other common initiatives.
communityType.metaCommunity: Organization that groups people who run or represent other communities.
communityType.mutualAid: The priority is mutual support through forums, chats, lists or other channels.

eventFormat.title: How to choose the format
eventFormat.description: Think about how the community's main activity usually happens.
eventFormat.bullet0: In person: they have in-person meetups and usually don't livestream them.
eventFormat.bullet1: Online: their activity is mainly online.
eventFormat.bullet2: Hybrid: there are in-person meetups and they are usually also livestreamed.
eventFormat.bullet3: Unknown: if you don't have enough context.

location.title: How to indicate the location
location.description: Indicate the most useful geographic reference for understanding where the activity happens.
location.bullet0: Use city or main region in a format like `City, Country`, for example `Barcelona, Spain`.
location.bullet1: Use `Itinerant` when the community changes city or venue depending on the edition or event.
location.bullet2: If you're not sure what value to put, it's better to open an issue to discuss it first.

parentOrg.title: What is an umbrella organization?
parentOrg.description: An umbrella organization is an entity that groups several local communities under the same network or brand (e.g. GDG Spain, PyLadies, Codebar). If your community belongs to one of these networks, select it here. The vast majority of communities have no umbrella organization.

shortDescription.title: How to write the short description
shortDescription.description: Summarize in one sentence what makes this community special.
shortDescription.bullet0: Indicate the organizational form if you know it: collective (without legal entity), non-profit association, foundation, cooperative, company with community activity, user group, etc.
shortDescription.bullet1: Prioritize what it offers, its focus or value proposition.
shortDescription.bullet2: Avoid repeating only labels, technologies or target audience that you've already marked above.
shortDescription.bullet3: An ideal length is usually between 140 and 220 characters.

geographicScope.title: Geographic scope
geographicScope.description: Which territory the community serves. It does not have to match where its events happen: a community can meet in Madrid and support people across Spain.
geographicScope.bullet0: Local: the community targets one town or metropolitan area.
geographicScope.bullet1: Province-wide: it covers a whole province.
geographicScope.bullet2: Region-wide: it covers an autonomous community.
geographicScope.bullet3: Nationwide (Spain): it covers the whole country, even if events cluster in one city.
geographicScope.bullet4: International: the community operates beyond Spain.

openData.title: Open data + AI
openData.subtitle: All {{total}} communities in the directory are open data. Download them, ask a chatbot about them, join them with your own data, or hand them to an agent. Please do.
openData.license: reuse, remix and redistribute, commercially too, as long as you credit Community Builders and link back to the directory.

files.llms: llms.txt — entry point for LLMs: what exists, where, and how to read it
files.csv: communities.csv — one row per community, for spreadsheets
files.geojson: communities.geojson — communities with coordinates, as GeoJSON
files.schema: schema.json — what every field and every value means
files.tags: tags.json — topic taxonomy, in Spanish and English (same ids)
files.llmsFull: llms-full.txt — the whole directory as Markdown
files.audience: audience.json — audience profiles, in Spanish and English (same ids)

code.lead: The files are plain statics served with open CORS, so you can fetch them straight from a script, a notebook or a frontend. They are regenerated on every deploy, so you always get the latest data.
code.gotcha: Two common traps: "tags" and "targetAudience" are ids (join them against tags.json and audience.json), and a generalist community carries an empty array plus "matchesAllTags": true. It is all documented in
code.hintShell: filter the dataset from your terminal
code.hintJs: resolve tag ids into readable labels
code.hintPython: load the CSV and group it

agents.lead: Building an agent, or using Claude Code, Cursor or similar? Paste these instructions into its context (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, system prompt or rules file). They tell it where the data lives and how to read it without getting it wrong.
agents.noMcp: No MCP server needed: the data is a set of public static files, so any agent with network access can read it directly.
agents.llms: machine-readable index of every file and how to interpret it.
agents.agentsMd: orientation for agents about to work on the repository itself.
agents.robots: crawling policy: every crawler, AI crawlers included, is welcome.
agents.instructionsHint: paste into CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or your system prompt

organizers.lead: More and more people look for communities by asking an AI. This is what makes yours show up well in those answers:
organizers.step1: Make sure you are in the directory and your record is current. If it is flagged as not reviewed by a human, review it: that field tells models how much to trust it.
organizers.step2: Fill in topics and target audience using the catalogue tags. They are what an AI uses to decide whether your community matches what someone asked for.
organizers.step3: Keep a working main URL and archive the channels you no longer attend. A dead link that looks alive sends people somewhere nobody answers.
organizers.step4: An Open Tech Events feed on your record puts your events in the directory, in aggregators and in front of any agent, and lets people subscribe without depending on whichever platform you use or on an algorithm. More reach, from the calendar you already keep.
organizers.note: None of this needs Git: the directory form opens the proposal for you and a person reviews it.
organizers.helpCopy: Questions about the events feed, the tags, the form or anything else in the directory: get in touch.

openData.footer: This dataset is maintained by volunteers and it is incomplete. If a community is missing or a field is wrong, fixing it is the most useful thing you can do.

attend.lead: Paste one of these into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity. Hit "Copy" straight away, or expand the block if you want to tweak it first.
attend.useTheSearch: For ordinary lookups — "Python communities in Valencia" — the search and filters on this site are faster and more reliable than asking an AI. These prompts are for what the directory cannot do yet: cross-referencing, telling community types apart, and finding your fit.
attend.note: If your chatbot cannot browse, download the file and attach it to the conversation. This data comes from volunteers: if something looks wrong or missing, please tell us.
attend.roadmap: We want the directory itself to do this without leaving the page: natural-language search and a statistics dashboard are on the roadmap —

found.lead: Starting a community begins with looking at what already exists: who else is trying, who could host you, and which gap is genuinely empty. These prompts answer that from the dataset instead of from a hunch.
found.note: Mind what the dataset does not know: no field says who hosts new groups or who is looking for people. That has to be asked, and these prompts are written to tell you whom to ask, not to guess the answer.
found.helpTitle: You do not have to start alone
found.helpCopy: This is exactly what Community Builders is for. Tell us what you want to start and we will put you in touch with people who have already done it, in your area or on your topic.

build.agentsTitle: If you build with an agent

prompts.rules:
Data rules:
- To recommend anything to me, only use communities whose "status" is "active". If I explicitly ask for dormant ones, label them as such.
- "tags" and "targetAudience" are catalogue ids. The catalogues exist in Spanish ({{tagsUrl}}, {{audienceUrl}}) and English ({{tagsEnUrl}}, {{audienceEnUrl}}): same ids, translated labels. Match against "label", "description" and "synonyms", not just the id.
- If "matchesAllTags" is true the community is generalist and fits any topic even with an empty list; same for "matchesAllAudience" and profiles.
- Coverage is uneven: many records are missing "tags", and most have no "targetAudience" or "geographicScope". An empty field means nobody has filled it in, not that the community has nothing to do with that topic: do not silently drop it, and tell me when the data is missing. {{indexUrl}} carries the exact count per field.
- "location" is where events happen; "geographicScope", where present, is the territory served.
- "lastReviewed" is the date the record was last checked, not an activity signal: most have not been revisited since they were added. The only field that evidences real activity is an events feed in "urls.ote".
- Never suggest URLs listed in "archivedUrls": nobody is listening on those channels.
- "humanValidated": false means a scraper filled the record in and no person has reviewed it. That is the majority: warn me.
- Do not fill gaps with things you know from outside the dataset. If a fact is not there, say so. If something has to be asked of the community itself, tell me and give me the channel.

tribe.label: Find my people
tribe.hint: asks about your profile, then recommends
tribe.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I want to find communities that fit me, not just my topic.

**Before recommending anything, ask me.** First look at what fields the dataset carries and at the topic and audience catalogues, then ask me the questions that genuinely help you narrow it down: which topics interest me, where I live and how far I can travel, whether I prefer in-person, online or either, what kind of community I am after (recurring meetup, conference, hacklab, mutual-aid group…), where I am in my career, which languages I speak, and anything else the dataset lets you cross-reference that would improve the recommendation. Keep it conversational, two rounds at most, and offer concrete options so I can answer easily.

Once you have my profile, recommend 5 to 8 communities ranked by fit. For each: name, city, why it fits me specifically, and its link. Then add 2 or 3 I did not ask for but that might surprise me, and say why.

{{rules}}

types.label: Which kind of community suits me
types.hint: the seven dynamics, and which one is yours
types.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} and the field dictionary at {{schemaUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

Communities do not all work the same way, and I want to understand the differences before deciding where to walk in. The "communityType" field sorts them into seven kinds, and schema.json explains what each value means.

**Before recommending anything, ask me**: what I am after (learning something specific, meeting people, building with others, asking for help, giving it, speaking in public), how much time I can give and how often, whether I want something recurring or one-off, and where I am.

Then, with my answers in hand:
1. Explain what each kind actually is — "tech-meetup", "conference", "hacklab", "umbrella-org", "collaborative-group", "meta-community", "mutual-aid": how it runs, what is expected of a newcomer, what commitment it usually asks for, and how many of each the dataset holds. Keep it short and comparable, not a paragraph each.
2. Tell me which two or three kinds fit what I described, and why you are ruling the others out.
3. Suggest three or four specific communities of those kinds, near me or online, with their link and what to expect the first time I show up.

{{rules}}

speaker.label: Where to give a talk
speaker.hint: asks about your talk, then finds the fit
speaker.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I want to pitch a talk and I am looking for where it would land best.

**Before proposing anything, ask me.** Look at what the dataset and the catalogues contain, then ask what you need to get this right: what my talk is about and at what level, whether I have given it before or I am debuting it, which cities I can travel to or whether it is online only, whether I want a small meetup to road-test it or I am aiming straight at a conference, what language I give it in, and which audience I want to reach. Ask conversationally, with concrete options.

Then give me two separate lists:
1. **Recurring meetups** ("communityType": "tech-meetup"): because they come round often they need speakers continuously, which makes them a better place to debut.
2. **Conferences** ("communityType": "conference"): their call for papers usually opens once a year. The dataset holds no CFP dates: tell me what you can infer and send me to their site or events feed to check.

For each: name, city, why it fits my talk, its link, and where available its events feed ("urls.ote") or events platform ("urls.eventsUrl"). Finish with a plan: which ones you would start with, and in what order.

{{rules}}

volunteer.label: Lend a hand
volunteer.hint: plausible candidates, and whom to ask
volunteer.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I would like to volunteer with tech communities and events.

**Heads-up before you start: the dataset does not say which community is looking for volunteers.** There is no such field, so do not invent one. What I want is a short list of plausible candidates and the channel to go ask them myself.

**And before anything else, ask me**: where I live and how far I travel, how much time I can give and how regularly, what I can do or would like to learn by doing (day-of logistics, communications, web, finding speakers, welcoming newcomers…), and which topics interest me.

Then, using "communityType", give me two lists:
1. Communities that by their nature run on whoever shows up: "hacklab", "mutual-aid", "collaborative-group", and "tech-meetup" ones, which being recurring need hands continuously.
2. Conferences ("conference"), where volunteering tends to be one-off and clustered around the event date.

For each: name, city, why I might fit, and how to get in touch ("contactInfo" where present, otherwise the most appropriate channel in "urls"; if there is none, say so).

Finish by drafting a short introduction message I can adapt, one that asks whether they need help rather than assuming they do.

{{rules}}

synergies.label: Synergies for my community
synergies.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I run a community and I am looking for collaboration opportunities.

**Heads-up: the dataset does not say who is open to collaborating.** There is no field for it. Give me candidates by affinity — topic, area, community type — and assume the interest itself has to be asked about; do not present it as a fact.

**Before analysing anything, ask me.** First work out which community is mine (search the dataset by name and show me the record so I can confirm), then ask what you need: what kind of collaboration I am after (joint event, speaker exchange, promotion, sharing a venue), whether I want to stay in my city or reach others, what I am short of right now (attendees, speakers, hands, visibility), and whether I would consider absorbing or reviving a dormant community.

Then give me three lists:
1. Active communities worth doing something joint with: adjacent but not identical topic, compatible area.
2. Communities on my topic in other cities, in case a speaker tour or a multi-venue event makes sense.
3. Communities with "status": "inactive" in my area or topic that might be revived, with the channel they had. Remember "lastReviewed" is no proof they are still dormant: tell me to check before writing.

Finish with the concrete first step for each of the three: whom I write to, through which channel, and what I propose.

{{rules}}

gaps.label: Gaps in the ecosystem
gaps.hint: what is missing, where, and what cannot be known
gaps.text:
Read {{indexUrl}}: it is the open-data index for the directory of Spanish tech communities. Follow it to whichever files you need.

I am thinking about starting a community and I want to know what is actually missing before deciding what. If narrowing it helps — one region, one family of topics, one audience profile — ask me first where to focus; otherwise do the whole thing.

Give me:
- Active communities per province and per autonomous region.
- Over-represented topics, and topics with very few or no communities, using the tag catalogue categories.
- Underserved audiences, joining "targetAudience" against the audience catalogue. First tell me how many records even carry that field: if they are few, this part is a hint, not a conclusion.
- Concrete gaps: topic-and-area combinations where nothing exists. If you weigh that with anything outside the dataset (population, local industry, universities), say so separately and cite where it comes from.
- Which part of the dataset is unreliable, using "humanValidated" and the coverage of each field.

Finish with the five communities that, if someone founded them tomorrow, would close the biggest gap, and what would need verifying before anyone tried. And tell me what you cannot be sure about from this data.

{{rules}}

umbrella.label: Who could host or back me
umbrella.hint: umbrellas, hacklabs, and communities to revive
umbrella.text:
Fetch {{dataUrl}} (open data from the directory of Spanish tech communities, CC BY 4.0).

I want to start a community and I would rather not begin from scratch on my own: before inventing anything, I want to know who is doing something similar and who could host or back me.

**Heads-up: the dataset does not say whether an organisation hosts new groups.** There is no field for it, so do not claim it. Give me candidates and the channel to ask.

**Before anything else, ask me**: what I want to start and where, what I am missing (a venue, reach, a legal umbrella, experienced people, speakers), whether I already know of something similar, and how much time I can sustain.

Then give me:
1. Whether something identical or very close already exists in my area: sometimes joining beats duplicating. Tell me even if it is not what I want to hear.
2. Umbrella organisations ("umbrella-org") and meta-communities ("meta-community") on my topic or in my area: they are the ones that group or coordinate others, and the ones who best know what has already been tried.
3. Hacklabs and physical spaces ("hacklab") where a new activity could fit.
4. Dormant communities ("status": "inactive") on my topic and area: reviving something that already has a name and people around it costs less than founding one. Give me their channel, and remind me "lastReviewed" is no proof they are still dormant.

Finish with a first-steps plan: whom I write to first, what I ask, and in what order.

onboarding.label: Brief your agent
onboarding.hint: what exists, and what you can promise
onboarding.text:
Read {{indexUrl}} and {{schemaUrl}}: they are the open-data index for the directory of Spanish tech communities and the dictionary of its fields. From the index you reach everything else: the JSON dataset, the CSV, the GeoJSON, the topic and audience catalogues, and the full dump as Markdown.

**Before writing a line of code, ask me** what I am building (a directory, an events aggregator, a bot, a one-off analysis), on what stack, and whether I need the data live or a copy will do.

Then, still without code, summarise for me:
- Which files exist, what each one holds, and which suits my case.
- Which fields I can rely on and which are sparsely filled, with the counts the index itself gives. I want to know what I must NOT promise in my product.
- The data-model traps that would make me display things wrongly.
- What the CC BY 4.0 licence asks of me: how I attribute and where I link.
- That the directory stores no events: each community publishes them in its Open Tech Events feed ("urls.ote"), so events are aggregated from there.
- How a wrong record gets corrected, so my project gives value back instead of only consuming.

Once that is clear, propose the simplest way to start, and tell me what to cache and how often to refresh it.
